item.title: The cognitive dissonance election
item.description: Democrats like what the polls say. They’re just not sure they believe them. Plus, Still Counting EP8 and our Election Night plans.
item.content:encoded:
This is the weekly Still Counting post. It’s coming to you a day late because yesterday was one of those days. Not in a bad way, but in the way the last few days before the election typically are.

We’re in a mode now where we’re sort of a tapas restaurant and are going to deliver posts to you as they become available from the overburdened kitchen. We’ll try to space things out, but it’s possible that dishes will pile up and there will be some dry spells, or that you’ll get more than one newsletter or more than one FLIPR update in a day.

The one constraint that’s absolutely locked into place is our Election Day coverage:

  • In line with FiveThirtyEight/Silver Bulletin tradition, shortly after midnight on Tuesday, we’ll run the final FLIPR update of the season and post our final overview of the race.1

  • Then we’ll lie in bed “sleeping” as we refresh Twitter constantly.

  • We’ll spend the afternoon nervously pacing around while trying to ignore anecdotal reports about turnout in Waukesha County.

  • Then starting at roughly 5:30 pm, we’ll be co-hosting an Election Night video stream and liveblog with The Argument, Galen Druke’s GD Politics and Matt Yglesias’s Slow Boring, plus plenty of special guests. Like it says on the invites to cool parties (not that I’d know anything about those) we’ll go from 5:30 until “late,” although we’ll preserve some energy if the outcome is ambiguous and it looks like vote-counting has slowed to a crawl.

We tested the liveblogging tech last night, and it went relatively smoothly. We’re super excited about this feature, and grateful to Substack for developing it. We hope to employ it for things other than Tuesday too, like big political or sports nights.

The intent for Election Night is for the video stream to be free, while the liveblog, where we’ll get a bit more granular, will be for paying subscribers.2 We really hope that you’ll join us!

Subscribe now

Meanwhile, here’s the YouTube of the Still Counting episode:

And here’s the audio. We’re very grateful for any reviews, comments, likes and subscribes you might spare.

The context

When FLIPR launched in August, I wrote that this wasn’t an election that filled me with a sense of “existential dread,” compared with… well, most of the recent ones. We knew both background conditions and midterm history were on Democrats’ side. If anything, those indicators have been unusually self-consistent this cycle. It was safe to assume Democrats were clear favorites to flip the House — you didn’t need FLIPR to tell you that, really, considering that Republicans started out with such a small majority — along with a number of governorships and state legislatures.

But in the Senate, we were caught between the proverbial rock and a hard place, since the battlegrounds required for a Democratic majority were being contested in very red terrain. Were Democrats really going to win Texas? Or Kansas? Or Alaska?

FLIPR initially forecasted the Senate odds at close to 50/50. As in 2024, that had seemed to make this election something of a low-stakes affair for the model. 28,000 lines of code, and all FLIPR was really saying is “well, who knows?”

Then, within a couple of weeks of Labor Day, there was some kind of phase change, with Democrats gaining 2 to 3 points on the generic ballot. There were several logical reasons for this: rising gas prices, further declines in Trump approval, growing evidence of a Democratic enthusiasm advantage, and perhaps increased public concern about AI, an issue where Trump is on the wrong side of the consensus.

So we’re no longer in the safe, nothing-ventured, nothing-gained “toss-up” zone. Democrats moved up to being roughly 3-to-1 favorites in FLIPR, and they’ve basically remained there for a few weeks now.

If you squint, there’s actually been the slightest recovery for Republicans on the generic ballot — but I’d argue that state and district polls have, if anything, been getting better for Democrats, like in a set of CNN polls yesterday morning that had them winning Kansas by 4 points and Texas by 6 (!). Even South Carolina might be in play, a flip I was (and to some degree remain) skeptical about.

Don’t believe polls from CNN or the NYT? Well, look at the New York Times polling database, where we get most of FLIPR’s data from, and search for any poll showing “Republican sponsor.” The GOP-commissioned polls3 imply a Senate map that is at best a toss-up for Republicans, but really leaning D, along with deep prospective gains for Democrats in the House and bad results for Republicans in swing-state governorships.

In a twist that I’m not sure I’ve seen before, Republican “vibes” about this election — especially if you adjust those partisan polls for the usual partisan bias4 — almost seem to imply a worse outcome for Republicans than Democratic ones.

But just look at where Republicans are spending money: it implies a deeply defensive, almost “prevent defense” posture. Or look at how Democrats are trying to expand the map in the House. There’s some kind of disconnect here between stated beliefs and revealed preferences.

I don’t have as much time to go into a deep-dive about the psychology here as I’d like. But I think Democrats are treating the possibility of flipping the Senate as "found money.” They’re optimistic-ish, but they don’t want to get their hopes up too much. It’s easy to understand why:

  • 2016

  • Despite Joe Biden’s win that year, 20205

  • And to a slightly lesser extent, 2024

Still, it’s one thing to take a healthy attitude of “hope for the best, but be prepared for the worst,” and another to actually have to put odds on the outcome, as FLIPR and people trading at prediction markets do. Some of the gaps between models and markets that we’ve previously highlighted have narrowed significantly.

But it remains hard to wrap your head around this election because it feels so boom-or-bust:

This is an understandable sentiment, and the “boom” part is true. Conditional upon James Talarico winning in Texas — Texas! — Democrats will be huge favorites to flip the Senate. Specifically, around 90 percent of the time according to FLIPR Deluxe.

But if Democrats don’t win Texas?

What might be counterintuitive is that they’ll retain decent chances of winning the Senate. Democrats could flip the Senate solely by winning states that Barack Obama won at least once: North Carolina, Maine, Ohio and Iowa. (They’d also, nontrivially, have to hold all of their own seats.) There are also more exotic possibilities: Alaska, Kansas, Nebraska, South Carolina or maybe even Montana.

FLIPR polling averages show Mary Peltola and Adam Hamilton slightly ahead in Alaska and Kansas, respectively. Nebraska is basically a tie in the polls between Pete Ricketts and Dan Osborn, although the advanced features of FLIPR shift Nebraska to Lean R.

But here’s where I think some of the cognitive dissonance creeps in. It’s easy to say: “well, either there will be a polling bust” — indeed, such an occurrence is highly plausible! — or “polls are basically right, so Democrats will win and maybe run up the score.” Ergo, the Senate is 50/50, you might think.

That’s not the worst first approximation, but it leaves a lot out. Those outcomes aren’t necessarily equally likely, and this election isn’t necessarily that binary. Democrats might be able to withstand a modest polling error in the Senate. Or polls could underestimate them, like they did in 2025.

Or the outcome might just get a bit weird. I wouldn’t really be that surprised, for instance, if Talarico wins — but Susan Collins wins too.

Election observers might actually be overindexing to presidential years, when there are the same two candidates on the ballot at the top of the ticket, and race-by-race correlations are stronger than in midterms. Because they lead in the polls, however narrowly, in states totaling 54 Senate seats — 55 if you count Nebraska, where Osborn is 0.3 points “ahead” in our polling average6 — most of the weird outcomes result in D wins, in the same way that being a field goal ahead is nice if the second half of an NFL game turns into a comedy of errors.

At the same time, there isn’t any sort of “safe space” here. There’s no “Blue Wall” or anything like that. Except probably for North Carolina, none of the prospective D pickups are “safe” or “solid.” I have my opinions about which pickups are relatively more likely and relatively less likely, and FLIPR does too.

But this requires a willingness to “trust the process,” when Democrats very understandably feel like the polls are Lucy with the Football. And even FLIPR can only provide conditional, probabilistic affirmation. A roughly 3-in-4 chance means that you’ll lose 1 in 4 times: all it takes is the coin coming up tails twice in a row.

It’s more natural to compare 2026 to other midterms. But in certain ways, the best analogy is to a presidential year, 2008, the last time the political environment was polling so blue. Barack Obama flipped several states — Virginia, Colorado, North Carolina and oddly, Indiana — that at the time were considered canonically, almost existentially Republican. (Those states have taken different trajectories since then, obviously.) Or if you prefer, FLIPR’s forecast is a bit like picking the Knicks to win the NBA title or the Milwaukee Brewers to win the World Series after they’d won the first two games of the series. “I’ll believe it when I see it” is the attitude people take when it comes to things like this, and I don’t blame them exactly.

Are pollsters herding? And if so, toward what?

On Still Counting, we discussed a Marist poll that came out this week and had some very weird results in Maine. This now feels like slightly old news. But the poll showed Troy Jackson ahead by 9 points among registered voters and the Democratic gubernatorial nominee, Hannah Pingree, up by 11 among RVs. Among likely voters, however, Marist showed Jackson at a mere +2 — and Pingree tied against Republican Bobby Charles.

I’m not one to critique individual polls. Since we’re publishing a lot of newsletters, and since I tweet a lot, I think I’ve established some credibility on that front. But as I said on the show, I don’t think the Marist poll is defensible.

It’s not that Jackson +2 is infeasible. Indeed, it’s very close to FLIPR’s forecast in ME-SEN! What I don’t buy, though, is that Jackson would win by 9 points if every registered voter turns out, but is only slightly ahead given the actual likely-voter Maine electorate.

But ignore the Senate race for now, as important as it is. Marist’s gubernatorial poll in Maine makes absolutely zero sense.

For one thing, no other poll shows anything remotely in the vicinity of a tie in the governor’s race. Pingree leads by roughly 10 points in our polling average, which includes the Marist poll — but no other poll this cycle shows Pingree anything less than 8 points ahead:

The whole question in Maine is whether Collins has retained her supernatural powers to outperform polls and partisan baselines in a blue state in what looks like a very blue environment. I actually might take the under on FLIPR’s roughly 70/30 odds for Jackson.

There shouldn’t be much question, though, about Pingree being a heavy favorite in a fairly typical gubernatorial race. True, governor’s races are less correlated with the overall partisan environment than races for Congress, but Charles is a fairly obscure opponent whereas Pingree comes from a locally popular mini-dynasty.

The topline in Marist’s RV numbers was:

  • Pingree, 51 percent

  • Charles, 40 percent

  • Independent Rick Bennett, 7 percent

  • And 2 percent undecided.

Maine, unlike (say) South Carolina, is typically a high-turnout state, with somewhere in the neighborhood of 70 percent turnout among registered voters in recent midterms. But suppose that 70 percent of Charles RVs turn out, along with only 60 percent Pingree’s supporters7 and Bennett’s supporters and undecided voters. This sort of spread is highly implausible, especially given that early voting looks decent-to-good for Democrats in Maine.

But humor me for a bit. Even with that correction applied, the topline would shift to Pingree 48, Charles 44. She’d still win.

I don’t see any way on earth that you have an 11-point shift from RV to LV in this relatively straightforward gubernatorial race, especially in what Marist itself sees as a D +8 national environment. On top of that, Marist has the undecided vote share in ME-GOV growing from 2 percent among registered voters to 6 percent among LVs. This makes even less sense. If you’re still undecided a week before the election, there’s a good chance that you won’t turn out at all. I’ve never seen a poll where the undecided ratio increased 3x when you filter for likely voters.

My leading hypothesis is that Marist, which does tend to publish relatively rosy numbers for Democrats, is terrified of its own shadow and/or terrified of being the next Ann Selzer, who was sued by President Trump. (The case was eventually dismissed.) The Senate race in Maine has a high profile; the gubernatorial race doesn’t. So it saw the Jackson +9 and it didn’t believe it, and then reverse-engineered its likely-voter model to produce a result that was more aligned with the consensus in Maine. And then its gubernatorial result was collateral damage.

My secondary hypothesis is that Marist’s spreadsheet or algorithm is broken and they ought to pay for some smart graduate students (or enough Claude or ChatGPT tokens) to fix it.

But if you’re issuing a survey that shows Pingree +11 and a tie in the same race in the same poll, you shouldn’t have published it.

Noah Wyhof-Rudnick has a great analysis of what pollsters are assuming about turnout shifts versus 2024. On average, the polls show a slightly more D-leaning turnout profile than two years ago, but only slightly.

You could argue that this is a conservative assumption given early voting data and other signs of Democratic enthusiasm. There’s also the potential issue, as Wyhof-Rudnick points out, of Trump voters mis-recalling or misstating their vote given how unpopular he has become, as some other pollsters have found. To simplify a bit, that could lead to these polls overestimating Republican turnout.

But, as Wyhof-Rudnick found, pollsters seem to be giving themselves varying degrees of permission to let their assumptions about turnout “float” relative to 2024, based on their priors about each race. They seem to be especially reluctant to underestimate Collins in Maine, given what happened in 2020.

This backs up my hypothesis, which is embedded into FLIPR, that pollsters are acutely aware of past polling errors and trying to correct for them — at the risk of either under-correcting or overcorrecting — and therefore the direction of polling error is hard to predict. Empirically, polling errors aren’t that correlated from cycle to cycle, but that might partly reflect how polling has become more of an art than a science. Human judgment plays a major role; as the Selzer Iowa poll in 2024 unfortunately showed, just “trusting your data” is no longer necessarily a reliable method.

Marist deserves credit for publishing both its RV and LV estimates, which most pollsters do not do. More often than not, the assumptions that pollsters make aren’t so transparent.

Still, I consider the Marist poll of Maine to be the “poll of the year.” Like Time Magazine's Person of the Year, this is sometimes an indicator of infamy, though. Pollsters seem to be undergoing a crisis of confidence and have a lot on the line (as do models like FLIPR). Polls are becoming something more like forecasts or models, rather than “pure” measures of public opinion. And models like FLIPR are becoming almost like prediction markets in basically taking a weighted average of those opinions. The Maine Senate race is a hard race to forecast. But I’m going to admit I’ll find it hilarious if Pingree wins by 10 points and Marist weighted its way out of what would otherwise have been an accurate result.

Silver Bulletin news and notes

  • We’ve patched FLIPR’s assumptions in the Montana Senate race, which is a weird one because there’s both an actual Democrat (Alani Bankhead) and a de facto Democrat (independent Seth Bodnar) on the ballot.

  • I’ve been doing lots of media, including being interviewed by Ezra Klein this week.

  • And please join us on Election Night!

Subscribe now

1

If you’re a pollster who happens to be reading this, please publish your surveys before 11:59 p.m. on Monday.

2

Subscribers to any of the four publications will have access to the liveblog.

3

Along with polls that aren’t officially Republican but usually lean that way.

4

Typically about 3-4 points of vote margin.

5

This actually featured the largest polling error of the Trump election triad.

6

Although not in FLIPR Classic and FLIPR Deluxe, which blend the polls with fundamentals and expert ratings, respectively.

7

The clause about “Pingree’s supporters” was unintentionally omitted upon first publication, which made this section ambiguous and confusing.

item.title: Could Haley Stevens cost Democrats the Senate?
item.description: Probably not, but let’s run the numbers on a rare *November* Surprise. Plus, please join us for our Election Night coverage!
item.content:encoded:
With 48 hours to go until votes begin to be counted on Tuesday night, I don’t really have time for anything other than full transparency. We’d planned to probably publish a second post today — please see our fun morning post with 13 quasi-randomly selected FLIPR maps — and this second post was originally slotted in as a relatively naked advertisement for our Election Night coverage, which we’ll be co-hosting with the good folks at The Argument, GD Politics and Slow Boring. If everything goes to plan, we’ll have both a (free) live video stream and a paid-subscribers-only liveblog.1 I’m mostly going to be focused on the liveblog component, but we’ll have plenty of insightful contributors for you on both channels.

I figured the post would start by talking about some of Sunday morning’s more interesting polls. But surprise #1: there weren’t many polls, nor were any of them all that interesting. Incentives in the industry are changing, and not necessarily in a good way. Sundays used to be big days for politics coverage back in the era of Sunday newspaper print editions and when shows like Meet the Press were incredibly influential. Now, the conventional wisdom seems to be that you fire out your best stuff on weekdays instead.2 Plus, high-quality polling is expensive, and pollsters may feel like they’re in a no-win position where they’ll either get accused of herding or risk publishing an outlier-ish poll that will surely get them criticized if they’re wrong — or who knows, maybe even sued by the president?

But then early this afternoon, we got a real surprise: Haley Stevens, whom Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated in the August Democratic primary for U.S. Senate, endorsed his Republican opponent Mike Rogers.

I’m going to be honest that I thought this was a fake headline when I first came across it on Twitter, sort of like I originally worried I might be hallucinating when I first heard about the Luka Doncic trade.3 I’m also going to be honest that I’ve sort of tuned out stories about the Democratic infighting in Michigan. Don’t get me wrong: we love talking about Democratic infighting at Silver Bulletin, love it, love it, love it. But it’s pretty much the only thing that anyone is going to be talking about in politics from early next year onward, when candidates begin to declare for the 2028 race, until the DNC in Boston, Denver, or Philadelphia in August 2028.

You can watch the Stevens video for yourself, but to me at least, she comes across as fairly petty and vindictive. To be fair, though, so has El-Sayed, who disinvited Stevens from campaign events. There’s not much maturity on display here. If Democrats had to do it over again, maybe they’d have nominated Mallory McMorrow, or begged Gary Peters to run for another term.

But could this actually swing the race?

Not that you should necessarily trust my instincts on this vibes-based stuff, but I’m of mixed minds here. Let’s start with the polls, where there’s good news and bad news for El-Sayed.

Good news for AES part #1a: he’s actually been expanding his lead over Rogers in recent surveys. Indeed, Michigan has been one of the better positive surprises for Democrats lately in polls that have mostly been fairly flat during the stretch run. Part #1b: he already has almost 50 percent of the vote. In fact, Michigan has among the fewest undecided voters4 of any Senate race at 4.8 percent; the lowest is Maine at 3.5 percent.

Now, polls can be wrong, of course. But even when they are wrong, it’s relatively uncommon for a candidate to finish with a lower share than their decided vote in the polls. Even Hillary Clinton didn’t do that: in 2016, she got 48.2 percent of the popular vote, versus 46.8 percent of the decided vote in the polls. (Donald Trump gained more ground, though still lost the popular vote.)

Indeed, FLIPR accounts for the number of undecideds. It’s a bit more confident about its forecasts when there are less of them, which is one of the reasons it’s had a pretty bullish forecast for El-Sayed.

Bad news for El-Sayed: look at the trajectory of the polls in that first chart. He was actually trailing Rogers back when he and Stevens were fighting in the summer before the primary was complete. So there’s at least some evidence that voters in Michigan are sensitive to Democratic unity, or the lack thereof.

To summarize my understanding of the impact of endorsements: the political science literature generally says endorsements aren’t that important unless they’re surprising, and this one was surprising. Or at least surprising-ish: tensions between the candidates had already been escalating and, as I wrote above, it hadn’t seemed to hurt El-Sayed in the polls; in fact, he was gaining ground.

There’s also the fact that roughly 1.9 million Michiganders have already voted, which might reflect something like 40 percent of the eventual turnout there, not counting voters whose ballots are in the mail but haven’t been counted yet. Now, generally speaking, undecided voters don’t vote early: rather, committed partisans do. But that blunts the effect, to some degree. It would probably have been worse for El-Sayed if this happened last weekend, in which case there would also have been more time for the story to metastasize in the national media. But now, newsroom resources are stretched thin as everyone prepares for Tuesday.

Even if this hurts El-Sayed with some voters, could it help him with others?

I won’t precisely share my Michigan mom’s reaction to hearing about the news today, but it did help to clarify one question for me. Are there any voters for whom this might reinforce support for AES?

I think it’s always important to ask this question when there is some sort of October/November Surprise. Let’s say that 3 percent of undecided voters5 are motivated to change their votes because of some breaking news, and they all move in the same direction — toward the Republican, say, after a late-breaking scandal involving the Democratic candidate. But suppose instead that, while 2 percent of those undecided voters lock in for the Republican, 1 percent move toward the Democrat instead. The net impact is now -1 instead of -3, only a third as much.

That might sound contrived, but take something like the Mary Peltola scandal in Alaska for reportedly being abusive to her staff. FLIPR now “officially” treats this as a scandal, even though it’s toward the lower wattage end as scandals go.

There are ways, though, that story might be read positively by an undecided voter in red Alaska. Peltola curses a lot, and she doesn’t have much patience for her overly sensitive, woke staffers, who complained about such things as being instructed to feed her chameleon.

Now, there is some legitimately bad behavior in the story too — she allegedly pushed a staffer. But there are probably some voters out there who read the story as a net positive. It sort of reinforces an image of Peltola being tough and not tolerating any bullshit. Indeed, you’d be hard-pressed to detect any net-negative fallout from it in Peltola’s polls:6

By contrast, take the FBI deciding to re-open an investigation into Hillary Clinton’s email server in late October, 2016. Maybe voters were going to care about that and maybe they weren’t. (Indeed, there’s good evidence that this did affect the race, maybe even decisively.) But nobody was going to think more positively about Clinton because of it. Indeed, some Democrats thought it actually hurt Clinton when she was eventually re-cleared simply because it recirculated the words “Clinton”, “FBI” and “email” in close proximity to one another in news headlines.

El-Sayed has been running against the Democratic establishment in Michigan, a state that has long had a penchant for anti-establishment, outsider candidates. Bernie Sanders won the state in 2016, Jesse Jackson did in 1988, and it was one of John McCain’s few wins against George W. Bush in 2000. Stevens famously became an avatar of the said establishment in a race where a major question was about AIPAC’s heavy spending on behalf of Stevens.

Then again, El-Sayed barely won that primary in what nearly was a massively wrong call by the polls. He’s frankly one of the weirder candidates we’ve seen in recent years: quite charismatic and very bro-y. But also he’s someone who can really get his back up instead of turning the other cheek. As someone who can be a bit confrontational myself, I sort of admire it in a weird way, but there’s a reason I’d never run for United States Senate. I don’t think there’s clear evidence on how this plays with voters; it would have been clearer if he’d won the primary by more.

Let’s turn to FLIPR

So let’s say the Stevens endorsement of Rogers reduces El-Sayed’s margin by 1 percentage point. If he’d been on track to win by 4 percent, now he’ll win by 3 instead, for instance. Or, if he was going to squeak by with an 0.5-percent victory, now he’ll lose by 0.5 points.

That 1-point swing is just an educated guess, and might be toward the higher side of my prior. Again: not many undecideds in Michigan, many people have already voted, the story might read positively for some voters, and many purported “game-changers” prove to be nothing of the sort. Weigh that against the fact that El-Sayed’s numbers did seem to suffer during the heat of the primary campaign in the summer. Let’s just stick with 1 percent.

How often, in FLIPR, did El-Sayed win Michigan by 1 point or less? In Saturday’s simulations, about 5 percent of the time. Again, AES does have some cushion in the polls. But if the polls are off, they might be so off that he was bound to lose anyway. It’s not quite that Rogers has to hit the bullseye, but it’s a pretty narrow target.

Next question: how often, in FLIPR’s simulations, did El-Sayed beat Rogers by less than 1 point and Democrats finish with exactly 51 Senate seats? In other words, a narrow win in Michigan that decided control of the Senate? That happened in 316 of our 40,000 simulations. So about 1 percent of the time, if you round up slightly.

(All of this is fairly linear, by the way. If you think the endorsement will hurt El-Sayed by half-a-point, the chances that it flips Michigan against him go down to about 2.5 percent, and the odds that it flips the Senate to 0.5 percent.)

So there’s a chance, indeed, that Haley Stevens just cost Democrats the Senate. It’s just not particularly high, unless your estimate of the endorsement’s importance is higher than mine.

This will complicate interpretations of Michigan, and not in a way that helps centrists

But suppose that El-Sayed does lose by a few tenths of a point. FLIPR doesn’t have him as that much of a favorite, and it’s probabilistic, but I’ll be honest that this is one of the “misses” that I’d feel relatively less bad about. FLIPR isn’t really equipped to handle late-breaking news that’s too late to show up in the polls. And our midterms model is generally less aggressive than our presidential one, which did move fairly aggressively against Clinton after the Comey news, for instance. So there’s a risk factor here that FLIPR is basically not capturing. I’m not going to manually intervene and subtract seven-tenths of a point from AES’s forecast or something like that.

Not that it’s your duty to care about FLIPR; that’s my job. What’s more important is the impact on the 2028 Democratic primary, where Michigan was already the most narrative-defining race. Now if El-Sayed loses, or wins but significantly underperforms Jocelyn Benson’s margin in the governor’s race or other partisan benchmarks for Michigan, progressives will have a ready-made excuse: Haley Stevens. They might even point to polls showing AES was on track for a clearer win before the endorsement.

This might be a dubious claim. If he loses, the polls might have been wrong all along, and El-Sayed was probably on track to underperform Benson anyway. But this was setting up as one of the cleanest tests in recent memory of whether progressives really do underperform moderates. Now the outcome is confounded. Maybe not hopelessly confounded: we’ll be able to look at things like how late-deciding voters made their minds up in exit polls and whether there was more D-to-R crossover voting than in other states. But confounded enough that moderates won’t be able to make quite as clean an argument if AES underperforms, especially since Democratic Party infighting tends to follow Calvinball rules anyway. Meanwhile, if AES wins by anything more than a point or two, he’ll look more formidable and Stevens and the establishment will look feckless.

A nerdy chat about the midterms

For those of you who want even more Silver Bulletin content, I figured it was worth posting the chat I had on Thursday with Galen Druke and Lakshya Jain of The Argument. Since part of our inspiration was to test out the tech for Tuesday night, this has mild “public access TV” vibes at times, but I think it was a good and substantive conversation that most of you will appreciate.

And we hope to see you Tuesday night — and before then. We’ll be posting FLIPR’s final forecast very early Tuesday morning, and should have another article or two for you in the meantime.

For full access to FLIPR and our Election Night liveblog, please consider becoming a paid subscriber.

1

Full disclosure: if for some reason the liveblog isn’t working, we’ll probably paywall the livestream too.

2

For what it’s worth, I think this is possibly wrong; Silver Bulletin posts that go up on weekends don’t show any meaningful underperformance relative to weekday ones.

3

It was a very late night and I’d played a lot of poker that day.

4

Technically, not all of these voters are undecided per se. FLIPR also lumps in voters for minor third-party candidates that we don’t model explicitly in this column.

5

I suppose my implicit presumption here is that the endorsement won’t flip many El-Sayed voters to Rogers (or vice versa) and that the impact will mostly be felt among undecideds. An actual vote flip costs twice as much as an undecided voter choosing a candidate.

6

I’d contrast this with the stories about operatives associated with Peltola recruiting other Dan Sullivans to be on Alaska’s ballot. Voters might not care about this much, but for the ones who do, it’s almost certain to be directionally negative for Peltola.

item.title: How to judge an election model
item.description: What would it mean for FLIPR to have a bad night? Plus, more on Haley Stevens and those NYT polls in Still Counting EP9.
item.content:encoded:
One more newsletter for you before we publish our final FLIPR forecast shortly after midnight. If you’re new here, we do not usually post this much: it’s typically ~3 items a week, not three a day. But we hope you’ll join us for our final flurry of coverage, including our Election Night livestream and live blog tomorrow.

Subscribe now

And we have a bonus episode of Still Counting out:

Reviews, comments, likes and subscribes are always greatly appreciated. Audio version here:

The context

We covered a lot of ground on the show. But I wrote about those NYT polls and Haley Stevens yesterday, so I’m going to use this as an excuse to cover another topic that Galen, Clare and I were only able to scratch the surface of. I thought it would be nice to write about this ahead of time so it doesn’t feel like spin if a lot of FLIPR’s forecasts don’t come true.

I’ll sometimes get the question, “How do you know if a probabilistic forecast is ever really wrong?” which is an entirely reasonable thing to ask. In fact, let me give you a four-part answer. It’s certainly not quite as simple as saying “30 percent chances are supposed to happen 30 percent of the time.” That’s true insofar as it goes, but it’s incomplete. And if you’re being Bayesian about it, you can’t always use this as a get-of-of-jail-free card. A 0.03 percent chance happening is much more suspect for your model than a 30 percent hitting.

First, the canonical way to answer this. You want your probabilistic forecasts to be well-calibrated over a sufficiently large sample of true out-of-sample predictions. In other words, if you’ve forecasted 100 events that you said had a 30 percent probability of happening, and 27 of them or 34 of them actually did “hit”, your model is doing well.

The “true out-of-sample predictions” part of the answer is important. Backtesting doesn’t count. Any halfway-competently-designed model should fit the past data well; that’s the easy part. But the model may be misfit or overfit, keying off of essentially random factoids in past data that have no true predictive power and aren’t likely to repeat themselves. You may have noticed that in documenting our models, we tend to not make claims like “ELWAY would have gotten the exact score right in the Super Bowl XVI” or “FLIPR would have nailed the 1994 midterm.” Who cares. We already know what happened. I generally think it’s a negative sign when forecasters brag about their backtested results instead of explaining why they think their models make structural sense.

In the case of the Silver Bulletin/FiveThirtyEight lineage of models, however, we have something fairly unique: an 18-year-track record of making true out-of-sample predictions in advance of elections and sporting events, which were published ahead of time, and indeed have received a ton of public scrutiny. At FiveThirtyEight, we actually had an interactive that diligently tracked our forecasts (although the Internet Archive version of the interactive is a little hinky and Disney nuked the original version). Our sports forecasts were extremely well-calibrated: over a large sample size, the 30 percent chances really did hit about 30 percent of the time, and so on. Our politics forecasts were pretty well-calibrated too, although actually a bit underconfident: there were actually too few upsets relative to what our models expected. It’s hard to know whether this is a statistically significant differential1, but it makes me a bit less worried when FLIPR is more confident about a race than the consensus.

A second way is a very Nate way that some of you won’t care for. Would the model have made you money if you’d been betting on it — relative to other models, the conventional wisdom as far as it can be sussed out, or betting markets? If you trusted our model in 2016, you should actually have made a large bet on Trump, because you could get roughly 5-1 or 6-1 odds when our model thought he’d win around 1 time in 3 instead.

We could get into a more detailed discussion about things like Brier scores — you not only want your model to be well-calibrated, you also want it to discriminate clearly between relatively more and relatively less likely outcomes. You’ll be calibrated perfectly if you always forecast every race as 50/50 but the model doesn’t tell you anything.

But I actually think some of the most important ways to evaluate a model are qualitative.

The third thing I always look at is whether a model responds proportionally to new evidence. If either the magnitude or certainly the direction of changes in our model doesn’t pass a common-sense test in accordance with the new evidence, that’s often a sign it’s poorly constructed.

For instance, when that set of very strong NYT/Siena polls for Democrats came out last night, their win probability in the Senate improved by about 2 percentage points in FLIPR. That seems fairly rational. Our odds for Democrats were already pretty favorable. And the NYT/Siena polls have generally been on the higher side of the averages for Dems, so FLIPR was expecting some relatively good numbers. Still, they’re a highly rated pollster, and their polls weren’t just good for Democrats but great in some states like Michigan, often showing favorable trendlines.

By the way, you can also kind of combine #2 and #3. Here, for instance, are Democrats’ Senate odds this year in FLIPR as compared to Polymarket:

This doesn’t always happen, but FLIPR has been leading Polymarket this year, you might notice. They’re going to wind up in roughly the same place, but FLIPR got there faster. Although I know this is self-serving, I’d argue that’s already a little bit of a “W” for FLIPR. (You could, in principle, have bought Democratic positions and sold/hedged them now to lock in a profit.)

Fourth and finally, you should make some effort to determine whether your model was lucky or good. This is sometimes easier in sports. With the Denver Broncos under Bo Nix, for instance, there have been some cases where ELWAY won its bet, but the team really had no business winning the game.

FLIPR has various hypotheses. Just to take a random few:

  • The incumbency advantage matters less than it once did.

  • State-by-state polling errors are correlated in midterms but not as much as in presidential years.

  • Gubernatorial races are less partisan than Congressional ones and produce more crossover voting.

Testable evidence for all of this exists in any given set of election results. If candidate quality matters less than FLIPR expects, maybe Ken Paxton and Roger Marshall hold on. If it matters more, though, maybe they lose but Susan Collins wins.

For all of this, by the way, margins ought to matter and not just the final calls. We’re quite skeptical about Democrats’ chances in Louisiana, for instance, but if Jamie Davis loses by just 1 point, that’s probably a bad forecast and not a good one even though our “call” will be right.

Conversely, some GOP Senate wins would be much worse for FLIPR than others. If Democrats pick up three Senate seats but lose recounts in Texas and Alaska, that’s much closer to FLIPR’s central distribution than if Roy Cooper loses North Carolina.

Possible FLIPR changes and improvements

What sort of things will we be looking to evaluate and potentially change in FLIPR and our other election models? Here are some things I’ve at least thought about. I always think it’s helpful to keep a mental list of these ahead of time so you’re not too overly driven by results and wind up fighting the last war.

  1. Whether to treat polling errors as being somewhat persistent, e.g., Susan Collins should get a boost because she beat her polls last time around.

  2. As discussed in SBSQ, whether to apply some sort of fancier adjustment for undecided voters, i.e., undecideds are presumed to be blue in Minnesota but red in Kansas.

  3. Whether to account for WAR or past election margins for non-incumbents; currently we’re only doing this for incumbents.

  4. Whether to include sources of fundraising other than individual contributions. Currently, we only include individual contributions and not things like PAC money. The individual dollars have been very lopsided in favor of Democrats this year, while the corporate and VIP money has gone the other way.

  5. Whether there’s some feasible way to account for candidate ideology in our “fundamentals” ratings. Currently, we only do this for incumbents, and it’s not really based on ideology per se but rather party loyalty in Congressional voting records.2

  6. Whether improvements could be made in our statewide partisanship scores, like accounting for the differences between midterm and presidential electorates, or changes in voter registration or migration patterns.

  7. Whether to remove the expert ratings layer from FLIPR Deluxe.

  8. Whether to force our estimate of the national House popular vote to more closely match our generic ballot numbers — currently, there’s a difference of about 1 or 1.5 points between these. This is intentional, not a bug, but it’s something we might examine if Democrats considerably outperform their popular vote forecast.

  9. Whether to account for early voting somehow.

  10. And this would be the big one if polls have a bad night: whether generally to de-emphasize polling in favor of other factors, and how that would be implemented, exactly.

But in each case, there’s at least some reason that we aren’t doing these things already. #5 and #6 would be nice, and probably helpful, but it’s not necessarily easy to find the right data, especially if we also need it for lots of past elections to help validate the model. I have a fairly strong prior against #1. For #4, the individual contributions data is nice to have as one of the relatively few objective non-polling inputs in FLIPR. Incorporating early-voting data (#9) would be a beast. It’s a moving target, and you’d need a lot of state-by-state customization; it might take months to do right.

Still, I do try to look at whether the sort of reasonable changes we could make but haven’t made systematically tend to favor one party or the other. Changes #1, #2, #4 and #10 would probably help Republicans this year. But changes #3, #5, #8 and #9 would likely help Democrats. It looks pretty even to me. I was slightly more worried when our model was more D than the consensus, but now prediction markets and other models have mostly converged toward FLIPR.

Of course, #10 is arguably as important as the other nine combined. FLIPR has actually moved slightly in the direction of being more fundamentals-based given the changes we made this summer. But it’s a bit truer to the polls than some of our competitors’ models, especially in estimating the national environment. However, models that make stronger assumptions about fundamentals and let them override polls are easy to overfit, and frankly have a middling-to-poor track record. Nor is it necessarily clear that this would help Republicans anyway, so maybe I was too quick to put #10 in their bucket. As I’ll argue in our closing story, there is lots of non-polling evidence supporting a strong year for Democrats too.
